passages.title: Oaths by the angels who manage souls and affairs
passages.tafsir:
Sūrat al-Nāziʿāt opens with five solemn oaths — five sworn descriptions of beings in ceaseless, urgent motion — building toward a single truth: the Resurrection is coming, and it is certain. What binds ayat 1–5 together is that, according to the overwhelming view of the early authorities, all five oaths describe **the angels**, and especially the angels of death, traced through the arc of their work: seizing the soul at death, carrying it up through the heavens, racing it to its destination, and then arranging what Allah has commanded for it there.

## Why swear by the angels at all?

In Arabic rhetoric an oath (*qasam*) lends weight to a claim the audience resists. Here the claim is the Resurrection itself, which the idolators of the Quraysh — and whoever rejects the Hereafter as they did — considered farfetched. Ibn Kathir titles this whole opening "Swearing by Five Characteristics that the Day of Judgement will occur."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes something subtle: the actual subject of the oath — the thing being sworn *to* — is not spelled out in ayat 1–5. It has been "contextually deleted," left unstated for the context to reveal. And it explains why *angels* are the fitting witnesses for this particular oath: they are involved at every moment in the administration and running of the world, executing their duties loyally — and on the Day of Judgement, when all material causes are severed, it is they who will be involved in the unusual events of that Day. The beings who run the present order are made to testify to the order that will replace it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a second, more personal reason the oaths centre on the extraction of the soul: **every person's death is his own partial Day of Doom** — and the Resurrection *starts* with human death. This, it observes, has an important impact on a person's belief in Resurrection.

## The five oaths, word by word

The five descriptions form a sequence, and the Arabic words are chosen with great precision.

**Ayah 1 — *wa'l-nāziʿāti gharqā*, "By those who pull out, drowning."** *Nāziʿāt* comes from *nazʿ*, "to draw vigorously." *Gharqan* intensifies it: *gharq* here carries the sense of *ighrāq*, "to exert oneself much or to the utmost extent in the thing" — the Arabs said *aghraqa al-nāziʿu fi'l-qaws*, "he drew the bow with great vigour." Ibn Kathir records from Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, Masrūq, Saʿīd bin Jubayr, Abū Ṣāliḥ, Abū al-Ḍuḥā and al-Suddī that these are "the angels who remove the souls from the Children of Adam" — and among people are those whose souls are removed with such difficulty that it is as if the person is being drowned as the soul is removed. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identifies these as the angels of punishment who draw out the souls of the infidels vigorously and harshly.

**Ayah 2 — *wa'l-nāshiṭāti nashṭā*, "By those who free briskly."** *Nashṭ* means "to untie the knot" — specifically, to untie the knot of something containing water or air so that what is inside is *released easily*. It is a metaphor for the gentle drawing out of the believers' souls, the exact opposite of the harsh plucking of ayah 1. Ibn Kathir mentions from Ibn ʿAbbās that some souls the angels remove with such ease it is as if they were simply unravelling the person from his soul.

**Ayah 3 — *wa'l-sābiḥāti sabḥā*, "And by the swimmers, swimming."** *Sabḥ* is to swim or float — here, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, "to glide along swiftly as in the sea where there is no mountain barrier," like a strong swimmer who goes far in swimming or a boatman who moves directly towards his final destination. These are the angels of death who, having extracted the soul, take it quickly towards the sky. Ibn Masʿūd said plainly, "They are the angels," and similar statements are reported from ʿAlī, Mujāhid, Saʿīd bin Jubayr and Abū Ṣāliḥ.

**Ayah 4 — *fa'l-sābiqāti sabqā*, "And by the racers, racing"** — rendered in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān as "then proceed forward quickly." According to Divine instruction, the angels do not delay in transporting the souls of people to their good or bad abodes: the believer's soul is transported to the atmosphere and blessings of Paradise, the unbeliever's to the atmosphere and torment of Hell. That this refers to the angels is narrated from ʿAlī, Masrūq, Mujāhid, Abū Ṣāliḥ and al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī.

**Ayah 5 — *fa'l-mudabbirāti amrā*, "And by those who arrange affairs."** ʿAlī, Mujāhid, ʿAṭāʼ, Abū Ṣāliḥ, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, al-Rabīʿ bin Anas and al-Suddī all said: they are the angels. Al-Ḥasan added, "They control the affairs from the heaven to the earth" — meaning, by the command of their Lord, the Mighty and Majestic. That last clause matters for sound belief: the angels *manage* nothing independently; they execute what Allah commands. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads this fifth oath as the final stage of the soul's journey: the angels commanded to reward and comfort the deserving souls gather the means of reward and comfort for them, and those commanded to punish organize the means of that.

## What the sequence teaches: the two deaths

Read together, ayat 1–2 paint two utterly different deaths. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes them vividly. When the infidel's soul is to be extracted, the whole scene of the punishment of *barzakh* (the realm between death and resurrection) comes in front of him; frightened, the soul disperses throughout the body, trying to hide or escape — and the angels forcefully extract it "just as wet wool wrapped around a skewer is forcefully removed." When the believer's soul is extracted, the reward, the blessings, and the welcome news of the *barzakh* come in front of him, and the soul slips free like a knot being gently untied.

Two pastoral corrections follow from this, both drawn out explicitly in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān. First, the harshness and the smoothness are *spiritual*, not necessarily visible: often the soul of an infidel apparently slips out easily — but that ease is only what is perceived by the humans around the dying man; the pain is felt by the soul itself, and we are aware of it only because Allah has informed us of it in this verse. Second, the reverse: there may be a delay at the time of a righteous believer's death, and this must not be suspected to mean he is undergoing some sort of suffering, although physically it may seem so. We simply cannot judge a death by watching it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān concludes from these verses that reward and punishment take place **in the grave and the barzakh**, before the reward and punishment of the Day of Judgement — and that authentic Traditions give elaborate details of this, including a lengthy Tradition of Sayyidnā Barāʼ Ibn ʿĀzib cited in Mishkāt-ul-Maṣābīḥ with reference to the Musnad of Aḥmad.

On a finer point, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relays the analysis of Qāḍī Thanāʼullāh Pānīpatī reconciling two statements that both occur in the texts: that the soul is "in the grave" and that it is "in ʿilliyyīn" (the exalted abode). He distinguishes the refined bodily soul — which the angels transport, which experiences the grave's reward or punishment, and which remains connected with the grave — from the *rūḥ mujarrad*, the abstract spirit, which never dies, remains in ʿilliyyīn, and feels the effects of reward and punishment indirectly. The real nature of the connection between the two is not known to anyone; it is known to Allah alone. Both statements are thus true, each speaking of "soul" in a different sense.

## The oaths as summons

So the five oaths form one tight argument, and its subject — deliberately left unstated in these verses — is the certainty of the Resurrection, which the verses that follow will unveil. The same angels who are, at this very moment, drawing out souls harshly and gently, gliding swiftly through the heavens with them, racing them to their abodes, and arranging reward and comfort or punishment by their Lord's command — these are the sworn witnesses that the process they begin at every deathbed is real, and that what it points to is certain. For the believer, the oaths are not merely a proof but a summons: death is not an end but a handover into angelic custody, and which of the two extractions meets you — the drowning wrench of ayah 1 or the gentle untying of ayah 2 — is being decided now.

passages.title: The two Blasts and the deniers' mocking question answered
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

After opening with five solemn oaths by the angels (ayat 1–5), the sūrah now delivers what those oaths were sworn for: the Day of Resurrection is real. Ayat 6–14 form a single dramatic arc. First comes the event itself — two cosmic Blasts, one after the other (ayat 6–7). Then the camera turns to the people living through it: pounding hearts and downcast eyes (ayat 8–9). Then the scene shifts to the deniers in this world, mocking the very idea of being raised after death (ayat 10–12). And finally Allah answers their mockery with devastating brevity: it will take only a single Blast, and they will find themselves standing on the resurrection plain (ayat 13–14). The whole passage moves from cosmic upheaval, to human terror, to human denial, to the divine answer.

## The two Blasts (ayat 6–7)

Ayah 6 speaks of *ar-Rājifah* — rendered "the quaking Blast" — and ayah 7 of *ar-Rādifah*, the one that comes "followed by" it, the second Blast. Ibn Kathir records that Ibn ʿAbbās said, "These are the two blasts (of the Trumpet) — the first and the second," and Mujahid, Al-Hasan, Qatadah, Ad-Dahhak and others made similar statements.

Mujahid is reported to have anchored each word in a parallel verse elsewhere in the Qur'an. The first, *ar-Rājifah*, he connected to "On the Day the earth and the mountains shake" (73:14). The second, *ar-Rādifah*, he connected to "And the earth and mountains shall be removed from their places, and crushed with a single crushing" (69:14). The two names thus carry the sequence inside themselves: a quaking, and then that which follows it.

## Hearts and eyes on that Day (ayat 8–9)

Ayah 8 says hearts on that Day will be *wājifah* — trembling. Ibn ʿAbbās explained simply: "This means afraid," and Mujahid and Qatadah said the same. Ayah 9 turns to the eyes: *abṣāruhā khāshiʿah*, "their vision humiliated." Ibn Kathir explains that this refers to the eyes of the people: they "will be lowly and disgraced from what they will witness of terrors." Notice the Qur'an's method here — it does not describe the Day by cataloguing its scenery, but by showing you a heart hammering in a chest and a gaze that cannot lift itself from the ground. The inner state (fear) and the outer state (humbled eyes) together paint the whole person undone.

## The mocking question (ayat 10–12)

Then the scene turns to this world, to the people who found all of this laughable. Ayah 10 quotes them: "Shall we indeed be brought back from *al-Ḥāfirah*?" Ibn Kathir identifies the speakers as "the idolators of the Quraysh and whoever rejects the Hereafter as they did." They considered resurrection after being placed in *al-Ḥāfirah* — which the commentary explains as the graves — to be something farfetched; Ibn Kathir notes that this was said by Mujahid. Their question is not a sincere inquiry; it is a sneer. To them, resurrection after the destruction of their bodies and the disintegration and decay of their bones is simply impossible.

Ayah 11 sharpens the sneer: "Even after we are bones *nakhirah*?" Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujahid and Qatadah all said this word means "decayed," and Ibn ʿAbbās gave a vivid gloss: "It is the bone when it has decayed and air enters into it" — bone so hollowed and crumbled that the wind passes through it. Ibn Kathir also notes that the word has been recited another way: *nākhirah*. This is the deniers' strongest card: look at what death actually does to a body. How could *that* live again?

Ayah 12 gives their final scoff: "It would in that case be a return with loss!" Ibn Kathir cites Muhammad bin Kaʿb that the Quraysh said: "If Allah brings us back to life after we die, then surely we will be losers." There is dark irony in the line — they say it as a joke, meaning "what a losing bargain that return would be," yet their words are truer than they know: for those who lived in denial, the return really will be a return into loss.

## The answer: one Blast, and it is done (ayat 13–14)

Allah's reply to all this scorn takes exactly two short ayat. "But it will be only a single *Zajrah*. When behold, they are at *as-Sāhirah*." The deniers imagined resurrection as an impossibly laborious reversal of decay. The answer speaks instead of a single Blast. Ibn Kathir explains: this is a matter from Allah "that will not occur twice, nor will there be any opportunity to affirm it or verify it" — no rehearsal, no second attempt needed. Allah will command the angel Israfil to blow into the *Ṣūr* (the Trumpet), and that blowing will be the resurrection itself: "the first people and the last people will all be standing before their Lord, looking."

Ibn Kathir stitches this to a thread running through the whole Qur'an: "On the Day when He will call you, and you will answer with His praise... and you will think that you have stayed but a little while" (17:52); "And Our commandment is but one, as the twinkling of an eye" (54:50); "And the matter of the Hour is not but as a twinkling of the eye, or even nearer" (16:77). One blast of the Trumpet, and the debate is over.

**Where will they find themselves?** *As-Sāhirah*, ayah 14, rendered in the translation as "above ground." Ibn ʿAbbās said it means "the entire earth," and Saʿīd bin Jubayr, Qatadah and Abu Salih said the same; ʿIkrimah, Al-Hasan, Ad-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd said it is "the face of the earth." Mujahid added a striking image: "They will be at its lowest part, and they will be brought out to its highest part" — from the depths of the graves to the open surface — and he described *as-Sāhirah* as "a level place." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the word refers to the surface of the earth: when the earth is re-created at the Resurrection it will be a completely level surface — no mountain barriers, no buildings, no caves — and this open plain of the Gathering (*ḥashr*) is what *sāhirah* names. The very people who asked "shall we be brought back?" will, in one instant, be standing on open ground with nowhere to hide.

Ibn Kathir also records a deeper point from Ar-Rabiʿ bin Anas: this plain will not simply be our familiar earth. He connected the verse to "On the Day when the earth will be changed to another earth and so will be the heavens, and they will appear before Allah, the One, the Irresistible" (14:48), and to the verses about the mountains being scattered as dust and left "a level smooth plain... nothing crooked or curved" (20:105–107). The earth brought forth on that Day, he said, will not be considered from this earth of this life: it will be an earth "that no sin will be performed on it, nor will any blood be shed upon it." The stage of judgment will itself be clean of everything that made judgment necessary.

## A word of consolation — and what the passage asks of us

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a tender historical note at the close of this section: the Prophet ﷺ used to be hurt by the stubbornness of these obstinate rejecters of the Resurrection. That is why the very next verses of the sūrah turn to the story of Mūsā (peace be upon him) and Firʿaun — to console him ﷺ, to show him that this hostility was not aimed at him alone, that the prophets before him faced the same and endured it with patience, and that he too should hold to patience and fortitude.

For the reader, the passage leaves two impressions to carry. First, the deniers' argument — "decayed bones cannot live" — sounds rational but rests on a false premise, measuring Allah's act by human effort; the answer, "only a single Blast," dismantles it without ceremony. Second, the trembling hearts and lowered eyes of ayat 8–9 belong to those who spent this life mocking that Day. The time to let one's heart tremble before Allah is now, while trembling can still change something.

passages.title: Moses called at Tuwa and sent to Pharaoh
passages.tafsir:
# Sūrah al-Nāziʿāt (79), Ayat 15–20 — Mūsā Called at Ṭuwā and Sent to Firʿawn

This passage opens the story of Mūsā (Moses, peace be upon him) at the moment his prophethood began: Allah calls him in the sacred valley of Ṭuwā and sends him to Pharaoh with a message of astonishing gentleness — an invitation to purify himself and come to know his Lord. What binds ayat 15–20 together is a single commissioning scene: the call (15–16), the assignment (17), the exact words Mūsā is to say (18–19), and the proof he is given to back them (20). The Qurʼān tells it here, in a sūrah about Resurrection, for a very deliberate reason.

## Why this story, and why here

The preceding ayat of Sūrat al-Nāziʿāt describe the deniers of Resurrection and the Day they dread. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the placement: the Prophet ﷺ used to be hurt by the stubbornness of the obdurate rejecters of Resurrection, and these verses recount the story of Mūsā and Firʿawn (Pharaoh) to console him — to show him that this hostile attitude was not aimed at him alone. Previous prophets faced the same, and they endured it with patience; the Prophet ﷺ too should exercise patience and fortitude.

Ibn Kathir draws out the second edge of the same lesson in his opening summary of the story. Allah informs His Messenger Muhammad ﷺ about His Messenger Mūsā: He sent him to Firʿawn and aided him with miracles, yet Firʿawn continued in his disbelief and transgression until Allah seized him with a mighty and powerful punishment. "Thus," Ibn Kathir writes, "is the punishment of whoever opposes you and rejects that which you have been sent with." The story is comfort for the believer and warning for the denier at once — which is why, as Ibn Kathir notes, Allah closes the account (in ayah 26) with *inna fī dhālika la-ʿibratan li-man yakhshā*, "In this is a lesson for whoever fears."

## The call at Ṭuwā (ayat 15–16)

Ayah 15 opens with a question addressed to the Prophet ﷺ: "Has the story of Mūsā reached you?" Ibn Kathir explains this simply as "have you heard of his story?" — a way of opening a narration that draws the listener in and signals that something weighty follows.

Then ayah 16: "when his Lord called him in the sacred valley of Ṭuwā." Ibn Kathir's gloss on *nādāhu* ("He called him") is precise: "He called out **speaking to him**." This is the moment of direct divine address to Mūsā. The valley is described as *al-muqaddas*, which Ibn Kathir explains as "purified" — a sacred, cleansed place. And *Ṭuwā*, he says, "according to what is correct, is the name of a valley, as preceded in Sūrah Ṭā Hā" — that is, the correct view among the explanations is that Ṭuwā is simply the proper name of that holy valley.

## The mission: a man who has "transgressed all bounds" (ayah 17)

The command is stark: "Go to Firʿawn; verily, he has transgressed (*ṭaghā*)." Ibn Kathir unpacks *ṭaghā* in three words: Firʿawn had become "haughty, rebellious and arrogant." This is the Qurʼān's diagnosis of the man before Mūsā ever meets him — the problem is not ignorance to be cured by information, but arrogance that has burst every limit.

## The gentlest words for the hardest heart (ayat 18–19)

Notice what Allah tells Mūsā to actually say. Not a threat, not a denunciation, but a question, an offer: "Would you be willing to purify yourself, and that I guide you to your Lord, so that you fear Him?"

Three movements are packed into these two ayat, and Ibn Kathir opens up each one:

- **Purification (*tazakkā*, ayah 18).** "Say to him: will you respond to the path and way that will purify you?" — meaning, Ibn Kathir explains, "will you submit (accept Islam) and be obedient?" The call to Firʿawn is framed first as something *for him*: a cleansing of his own soul.
- **Guidance (ayah 19).** "And that I guide you to your Lord" — meaning, Ibn Kathir says, "I will guide you to the worship of your Lord." Mūsā offers himself as a guide, and the destination is worship of the Lord to whom Firʿawn, like every creature, belongs.
- **Fear (*fa-takhshā*, ayah 19).** The goal of it all: "so that you fear Him." Ibn Kathir's explanation here is one of the most beautiful lines in his commentary on this sūrah: "so that your heart will become humble, obedient, and submissive to Him **after it was hard, evil, and far away from goodness**." *Khashyah* — reverent fear of Allah — is not presented as terror but as the softening of a hardened heart into humility.

## The great sign (ayah 20)

"Then he showed him the great sign." Ibn Kathir explains: Mūsā showed Firʿawn — along with this truthful call — "a strong evidence and a clear proof of the truthfulness of what he had come up with from Allah." The invitation was not left bare; it came backed by unmistakable proof. Gentle words and a great sign together: that is the whole of what this passage records Mūsā bringing to the tyrant's court. How Firʿawn answered, and what became of him, the ayat that follow will tell — and Ibn Kathir's summary has already warned us that his disbelief ended in a mighty punishment.

## Living it

Three things this passage asks of a believer, each drawn straight from what the sources say:

- **Patience under rejection.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān tells us this story was revealed to console the Prophet ﷺ and to teach patience and fortitude. Anyone who calls to good and meets stubbornness stands in a long line of prophets who met the same.
- **Gentleness in inviting others.** Allah sent Mūsā to a man He Himself described as haughty, rebellious and arrogant — yet with words of invitation: "Would you purify yourself?" — offering purification, guidance, and the softening of the heart. If that was the manner commanded toward Firʿawn, it is surely the manner owed to everyone else.
- **Ask for a soft heart.** Ibn Kathir's gloss on *fa-takhshā* describes what the reverent fear of Allah does: it makes the heart "humble, obedient, and submissive to Him after it was hard, evil, and far away from goodness." That transformation was held out even to Firʿawn; no heart, the offer implies, is too far gone to be invited back — and no reader should assume their own heart needs no softening.

passages.title: Pharaoh denies, claims lordship, and is ruined
passages.tafsir:
# Pharaoh Denies, Claims Lordship, and Is Ruined (79:21–26)

These six ayat are the climax and close of the story of Musa (peace be upon him) and Fir'awn that began in ayah 15. Musa has already delivered the invitation — "Would you purify yourself, and that I guide you to your Lord so that you fear Him?" — and has shown Fir'awn "the great sign" (ayah 20). What holds ayat 21–26 together is a single, terrible arc: Fir'awn's response, its escalation into an open claim of lordship, and the seizure by Allah that made him a warning for all time. The passage moves in short, hammering verbs — he denied, he disobeyed, he turned back, he strove, he gathered, he called out, he claimed — and then one decisive verb from Allah: *He seized him*.

## Why this story is being told to the Prophet ﷺ

Ibn Kathir opens his commentary on this section by explaining its purpose: Allah informs His Messenger Muhammad ﷺ about His Messenger Musa — how he was sent to Fir'awn and aided with miracles, yet Fir'awn persisted in disbelief and transgression until Allah seized him with a mighty and powerful punishment. Ibn Kathir then states the point plainly: such is the punishment of whoever opposes the Prophet ﷺ and rejects that which he was sent with. That is why the story closes, in ayah 26, with "In this is a lesson for whoever fears."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the tender, human side of this. The Prophet ﷺ used to be hurt by the stubbornness of the obdurate rejecters of the Resurrection. This story was recounted to console him: the hostility he faced was not unique to him. Previous prophets met the same adverse attitude and endured it with patience — and so the Prophet ﷺ too is being taught patience and fortitude. Read this way, the passage is not only a threat to the deniers; it is a balm for the one being denied.

## Ayah 21 — the anatomy of denial

"But he denied and disobeyed." Two verbs, and Ibn Kathir explains each: Fir'awn *rejected the truth* and *opposed what Musa commanded him with of obedience*. His heart disbelieved, and Musa's call could not affect him internally or externally.

Then Ibn Kathir makes one of the most penetrating theological observations in this whole section. Fir'awn *knew* that what Musa brought was the truth — yet that knowledge did not necessitate his being a believer in it. Why not? Because, in Ibn Kathir's words, recognition is the knowledge of the heart, while faith is the heart's *action*: to comply with the truth and submit to it. This is a crucial distinction for any reader. Iman (faith) is not mere intellectual acknowledgment that something is true; a person can be fully convinced and still be a disbeliever, because he refuses to yield. Fir'awn is the Qur'an's permanent proof of this: the evidence reached him, the recognition happened, and the submission never came.

## Ayat 22–24 — the escalation

Denial rarely stays still; it campaigns. In ayah 22, "then he turned back, striving" — and Ibn Kathir explains that his "striving" was in *responding to the truth with falsehood*. Concretely, this was his gathering of the group of magicians to confront the spectacular miracles Musa had brought. Fir'awn did not simply walk away from the truth; he turned from it and then worked energetically against it, mounting a counterfeit to compete with the sign of Allah.

Ayah 23 — "So he gathered and called out" — Ibn Kathir explains as Fir'awn gathering his people and calling out among them. And ayah 24 gives us what he proclaimed: "I am your lord, the most high." A created being, standing before people he ruled, claimed for himself the lordship that belongs to Allah alone.

Ibn Kathir preserves a striking report here from two early authorities. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid both said that this was the word Fir'awn said after he had said, "I have not known of any other god for you all other than me" (28:38), forty years before. The two blasphemies recorded in the Qur'an were not one outburst; they bookend four decades. This detail transforms how we read the passage: Fir'awn's ruin was not the punishment of a single rash sentence but of a long, entrenched rebellion. Allah's forbearance stretched across forty years of open tyranny — and denial, left unrepented, did not soften with time but grew to an even greater extremity.

## Ayah 25 — the seizure

"So Allah seized him, an exemplary punishment for the Hereafter and the first (life)." The key word is *nakāl*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān defines it precisely: an exemplary punishment — an extremely severe punishment given to an offender in order to *deter others* from committing a similar offence or sin. Fir'awn was not merely punished; he was made into a public, permanent warning.

The ayah names two punishments, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identifies them: the "punishment of the ūlā" (the first life) is what befell Fir'awn and his army in this world — destruction by drowning; the "punishment of the ākhirah" is what awaits him in the Hereafter. Ibn Kathir puts it in awesome terms: Allah avenged Himself against him with a severe vengeance and made an example and admonition of him for those rebellious people in the world who are like him. Ibn Kathir then links this ayah to two parallel verses: "And on the Day of Resurrection, evil indeed is the gift gifted" (11:99) — a curse in this world pursued by another in the Hereafter — and "We made them leaders inviting to the Fire, and on the Day of Resurrection they will not be helped" (28:41). The man who claimed to be "most high" became an example cursed in both abodes.

## Ayah 26 — who actually takes the lesson

"Surely in this is a lesson for whoever fears." Notice the condition: the lesson is only for "whoever fears." This closes a circle the passage opened earlier: Musa's original invitation to Fir'awn was "that I guide you to your Lord, *so that you fear*" (ayah 19) — which Ibn Kathir explains as the heart becoming humble, obedient, and submissive to Allah after being hard, evil, and far from goodness. Fir'awn refused that fear, so the story of his ruin now produces it in others. The very quality he lacked is the quality that unlocks the story's benefit.

## Living it

The passage leaves the believer with three concrete truths drawn straight from the commentary:

- **Knowing the truth is not the same as submitting to it.** Faith, as Ibn Kathir defines it here, is the heart's action — compliance and surrender — not mere recognition. Each of us must ask not "do I know this is true?" but "have I yielded to it?"
- **Delay in punishment is not approval.** Forty years passed between Fir'awn's two great blasphemies. Allah's respite is real, but so is His seizure — *nakāl* in this world and the next.
- **For anyone hurt by mockery or rejection for their faith,** the passage was revealed, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, to console the Prophet ﷺ himself: the prophets before him endured the same, with patience. The believer who fears Allah walks away from this story not crushed but steadied.

passages.title: Creating sky and earth proves resurrection is easy
passages.tafsir:
## One question that settles the whole argument

This passage is Allah's direct answer to the people who mocked the idea of resurrection. Having just recounted the destruction of Fir'awn (ayat 15–26), the sūrah now turns to the mockers themselves and asks a single, disarming question — *which was harder to create: you, or the sky?* — and then lets the built universe itself, from the raised heaven down to the pasture under their feet, make the case that raising the dead is no strain on the One who made all of this. Ayat 27–33 hold together as one sustained argument: a rhetorical question (ayah 27), followed by a tour of creation that answers it (ayat 28–32), sealed with a reminder of why it was all made (ayah 33).

## The doubt being answered

To feel the force of ayah 27, remember what the deniers had said earlier in this same sūrah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān connects this passage back to their scoffing question in ayat 10–11: "Are we going to be brought back to our former state? Is it when we will have turned into decayed bones?" As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, this was not a sincere question but a negative rhetorical one — their way of declaring that restoration to life after becoming perished, worm-eaten bones is simply impossible.

Allah's response, in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's words, is that the Supreme Creator "Who drew out this universe without any pre-existing matter and without any instrument, certainly has the Supreme power to give existence to things after destroying them. Why should it be a surprise?" That is the entire logic of ayat 27–33 in one sentence. The first creation was from nothing; the second is only a renewal.

Ibn Kathir frames the passage the same way: it comes "in refutation of the claim rejecting resurrection due to the renewal of creation after its original state." The question "Are you more difficult to create or is the heaven?" is addressed, he says, to people generally — 'O people' — and its intended answer is obvious: "rather the heaven is more difficult to create than you." He supports this with two parallel verses of the Qur'an: "the creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind" (40:57), and "Is not the One Who created the heavens and the earth capable of creating the similar to them? Yes, indeed! He is the Supreme Creator, the All-Knowing" (36:81). The argument is from the greater to the lesser: if Allah accomplished the greater work, the lesser cannot be beyond Him.

## How the passage explains itself

A beautiful feature of these ayat, which Ibn Kathir draws attention to twice, is that the Qur'an states something in general terms and then immediately unpacks it in the next clause.

**Ayah 27–28 — the sky.** Allah says *banāhā* — "He built it" — and then, as Ibn Kathir notes, He explains what that building means in ayah 28: "He raised its height, and has perfected it." Ibn Kathir describes the result: Allah made the heaven "a lofty structure, vast in its space, with equal sides, and adorned with stars at night and in the darkness." The sky is presented as architecture — built, raised, made flawless — precisely because the question of ayah 27 is about difficulty of construction.

**Ayah 29 — night and day.** "Its night He covers and He brings out its forenoon." The unusual verb here, *aghṭasha*, was explained by Ibn 'Abbas: "He did aghtasha of its night means that He made it dark" — and Ibn Kathir records that Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, Sa'id bin Jubayr and a large group of scholars said the same. So the meaning is: He made the sky's night intensely dark and black, and its day — its *ḍuḥā*, forenoon — bright, luminous, and clear. Even the alternation of darkness and light is part of the "building" of the heaven, run entirely by its Builder.

**Ayat 30–31 — the earth.** "And after that He spread the earth" (*daḥāhā*). Again Ibn Kathir points out that the general word is explained by what follows: the "spreading" of the earth means that "He brought forth therefrom its water and its pasture" — He brought out what was stored within it with a forceful action. The earth was not merely flattened; it was made livable, its water and vegetation drawn out of it.

**Ayah 32 — the mountains.** "And the mountains He has fixed firmly" — He settled them, made them firm, and established them in their places, so that, as Ibn Kathir explains under ayah 33, the earth "would be calmly settled with its dwellers," its dwelling places stabilized.

## "After that" — a note on the order of creation

Ayah 30 says the earth was spread *after* that — after the building of the heaven. Ibn Kathir addresses the apparent question this raises about the sequence of creation: it was mentioned previously in Sūrat Ḥā Mīm as-Sajdah that **the earth was created before the heaven, but it was only spread out after the creation of the heaven**. In other words, the ayah is not about when the earth came into existence but about when it was spread and furnished — its water and pasture brought forth. Ibn Kathir notes that this is the meaning of what was said by Ibn 'Abbas and others, and that it was the explanation preferred by Ibn Jarir. So there is no contradiction: creation of the earth first, then the heaven built and perfected, then the earth spread out and made ready for life.

## Ayah 33 — the argument ends in mercy

The passage does not close on raw power but on kindness: "As provision and benefit for you and your cattle." Ibn Kathir's comment here is expansive: Allah spread out the earth, caused its springs to gush forth, brought forth its hidden benefits, caused its rivers to flow and its vegetation, trees, and fruits to grow, and fixed the mountains so the earth would be calm for its dwellers. All of this is "a means of beneficial enjoyment for His creatures," providing for mankind and for the cattle they eat and ride — granted to them for the period they need them, "in this worldly abode, until the end of time and the expiration of this life."

Notice the two divine descriptions Ibn Kathir pairs at this point: He is "the Most Wise, the All-Knowing… Most Kind to His creation, Most Merciful." The same creative act proves two things at once — the power that makes resurrection undeniable, and the mercy that has been providing for you all along. And Ibn Kathir's closing phrase quietly returns to the sūrah's theme: these beneficial things are granted only for the period they are needed, "until the end of time and the expiration of this life."

## Where this sits in the sūrah

The placement of this passage is itself part of its meaning. Immediately before it, Allah recounts how Fir'awn — shown "the great sign" by Musa — denied, disobeyed, and proclaimed "I am your lord, most high," until "Allah seized him with a punishing example for the Hereafter and the first life" (ayah 25). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the word *nakāl* there as an exemplary punishment, one severe enough to deter others from the same crime — fulfilled in this world by drowning, with the punishment of the Hereafter still to come. "In this is a lesson for whoever fears" (ayah 26). Then comes our passage, turning from history to cosmos: the same Lord whom Fir'awn defied is the One who built the sky over your head. And immediately after it, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, the sūrah moves into the horrors of the Day of Judgment, when every person will be presented with his deeds, and the abodes of Paradise and Hell are described. Ayat 27–33 are thus the hinge: they establish that the Day the mockers denied is coming — because the One who promises it has already done something greater.

## Living it

The passage asks for one honest act of reasoning. The deniers' problem, as both commentaries present it, was never lack of evidence — Fir'awn saw the great sign and still denied, because, as Ibn Kathir observes in the preceding section, recognition is the knowledge of the heart while faith is its action: complying with the truth and submitting to it. So the believer's task with these ayat is to actually look — at the raised sky, the blackness of night giving way to the brightness of forenoon, the water and pasture drawn out of the earth, the anchored mountains — and let the looking end in submission rather than mere acknowledgment. Every one of these things was made "for you and your cattle": a daily, tangible kindness. The fitting response is gratitude toward the Most Kind, and readiness for the Day when the One who built all this brings you back — for the heaven was harder to create than you, and the One who accomplished the greater work is fully able to do the lesser.

passages.title: The Supreme Disaster and the two final abodes
passages.tafsir:
After recounting how Allah seized Firʿaun "for the deterrent punishment in the Hereafter and the present world" (79:25), and after answering those who denied the resurrection — for the Supreme Creator, Who brought this universe into existence without any pre-existing matter, certainly has the power to give existence to things after destroying them — the sūrah turns, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, to depicting the horrors of the Day of Judgement. On that Day every person will be presented with his deeds, and the abodes of the people of Paradise and the people of Hell are described. The passage sets two portraits side by side — the person bound for Hell (37–39) and the person bound for Paradise (40–41) — each, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes, marked by two characteristics, and each sealed with the same closing word, *al-maʾwā*, "the abode".

## The Supreme Disaster (ayat 34–36)

Ayah 34 names the Day of Judgement **al-Ṭāmmah al-Kubrā** — "the Supreme Disaster" or "Greatest Catastrophe". Ibn Kathir reports that Ibn ʿAbbās said this refers to the Day of Judgement, and explains why this name was chosen: it is called this "because it will overcome every matter. It will be frightful and horrifying." Ibn Kathir connects this to Allah's words elsewhere: "And the Hour will be more grievous and more bitter" (54:46).

Two things happen when that Day arrives.

First, in ayah 35, **memory returns**: "the Day every person will remember all their striving." Ibn Kathir explains that at that moment the Son of Adam will reflect upon all of his deeds, both the good and the evil. In this world we are experts at forgetting our own record; on that Day the whole ledger comes back at once. Ibn Kathir pairs this with a sobering parallel verse: "On the Day will man remember, but how will that remembrance avail him?" (89:23) — the remembering will come, but for the one who wasted his life, the time for acting on it will have passed.

Second, in ayah 36, **Hell itself is brought into view**: "and the Hellfire will be displayed for all to see." Ibn Kathir comments that it will become apparent to the onlookers, "so the people will see it with their own eyes." In this world Hell is a report we believe in without seeing; on that Day it is unveiled as a visible reality. The person standing there holds his whole life in his mind while the Fire stands in front of him — and the only question left is which of the two groups he belongs to.

## The one whose home is the Fire (ayat 37–39)

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that the people of Hell are described here by **two characteristics**, and the people of Paradise by two matching ones — and that these traits are given precisely so that "a man can decide in this very world" which abode he is heading toward.

The first trait, in ayah 37, is *ṭaghā* — "transgressed". Ibn Kathir defines it as the one "who rebels and behaves arrogantly." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills this out: instead of remaining loyal to Allah and His Messenger ﷺ and following their commands, such people adopt the line of rejection and rebellion.

The second trait, in ayah 38, is that he "preferred the fleeting life of this world." Ibn Kathir explains: he gives this world precedence "over the matters of his religion and his Hereafter." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the psychology concrete: if such a person faces a deed that gives comfort and pleasure in this world but punishment in the Hereafter, he prefers the comforts and pleasure of this life to the pleasure of the next.

For the one marked by these two qualities, ayah 39 gives the sentence: "the Hellfire will certainly be their home" — *al-maʾwā*, the abode, the place one finally settles and returns to. Ibn Kathir adds that in that final destination "his food will be from the tree of Zaqqum, and his drink will be from Hamim" — the bitter tree and the scalding drink of the Fire. The man who spent his life choosing comfort ends in the one place where no comfort exists.

## The one whose home is Paradise (ayat 40–41)

Against him stands the mirror image, also with two traits.

The first, in ayah 40: "as for those who were in awe of standing before their Lord" — *khāfa maqāma rabbih*, feared the standing before his Lord. Ibn Kathir explains: he fears the standing before Allah, and he fears Allah's judgement of him. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it vividly: in this life, he "shudders at the thought of appearing before Allah to account for his deeds on the Day of Reckoning."

The second trait: "and restrained the self from evil desire" — *nahā al-nafsa ʿan al-hawā*. Ibn Kathir explains: he prevents his soul from following its desires "and he compels it to obey its Master." The self (*nafs*) pulls toward what it craves (*hawā*, desire), and the believer keeps forbidding it and turning it back to obedience.

For this person, ayah 41 gives the matching promise in identical wording: "Paradise will certainly be their home" — and Ibn Kathir notes his final abode, his destination, and his place of return will be "the spacious Paradise."

## Two conditions that are really one

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out a subtle point: the verse lays down two conditions for Paradise, "but carefully considered, the two conditions, in terms of consequence, are one." The first condition is the fear of accountability in the presence of Allah; the second is to restrain oneself from evil desires — and, as the author says, it is in fact the fear of Allah that causes one to restrain oneself from evil desires.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then cites Qāḍī Thanāʼullāh Pānīpatī, who wrote in his Tafsīr Maẓharī that restraining the self from evil desires has **three levels**:

**The first level** is to avoid false beliefs that conflict with the express texts of the Qurʼan and established Sunnah and the consensus of the righteous predecessors. At this level a person deserves to be called a Sunni Muslim. Desire does not only pull toward sins of the body; it can pull toward beliefs as well.

**The second, middle level** is the daily battle: a person thinks of committing a sin, then remembers that he must account for his deeds before Allah, and abandons it. Its complement is to abstain even from *doubtful* things — acts about which one is not certain whether they are permissible, both possibilities being equal — and from permissible acts that might lead one to slip into the impermissible. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites here the narration of Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr that the Prophet ﷺ said that whoever abstains from doubtful things has protected his honour and religion, while whoever indulges in doubtful things will eventually indulge in forbidden things. Abandoning the doubtful and preferring what is definitely certain, the author says, is *taqwā* and the middle course of mastering the self.

**The third and highest level** is when, through abundant remembrance of Allah (*dhikr*), constant spiritual struggle against the evil passions (*mujāhadah*), and ascetic discipline, the self is so cleansed and purified that the desires tempting it to evil are totally eliminated. Of such people the Qurʼan says, addressing Shayṭān: "My servants are such that you have no power over them" (15:42). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also quotes the tradition that none of us can be a perfect believer unless the desires of his self follow what the Prophet ﷺ taught.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a warning that belongs with this ayah: the base self does not only push toward obvious sins. It smuggles its poison into *good deeds* — self-conceit (*ʿujb*), vanity (*kibr*), and showing off (*riyāʼ*) — sins whose sinful nature a person often cannot see in himself, "because he continues to think that his actions are right." Restraining the *nafs* therefore means suspecting it even when it is praying and fasting. The author counsels seeking sound spiritual guidance for this hidden struggle, and — for the one who cannot find such a guide — abundant *istighfār* (seeking Allah's pardon), noting the report that the Prophet ﷺ said he would recite istighfār a hundred times a day.

## Living it: you can read your own verdict

The most practical gift of this passage is stated by Maʿārif ul Qurʼān directly: these traits are portrayed "by which a man can decide in this very world whether, according to the rules, his abode would be Paradise or Hell." You do not need to wait for the Supreme Disaster to know which portrait you resemble. Ask the two questions of ayat 37–38 and 40: When my desire collides with Allah's command, which one wins? Does the thought of standing before my Lord actually change what I do?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful to say "according to the rules," because other verses and narratives show there can be exceptions — a person may attain freedom from Hell and enter Paradise through intercession or directly through the grace of Allah. But that is the exception; the general rule is the one these ayat put in our hands. And by the author's own summary, the rule comes down to a single spring of action: the fear of standing before Allah is what restrains the self from its desires — and for the one so restrained, the promise is that the spacious Paradise, not the Fire, will be the home he finally comes to.

passages.title: The Hour's timing is Allah's alone; the Prophet only warns
passages.tafsir:
# Sūrah al-Nāziʿāt (79), Ayat 42–46 — The Hour's Timing Belongs to Allah Alone

These five ayat close Sūrah al-Nāziʿāt as a single movement. The sūrah has just described the Great Catastrophe, the Day when man will remember what he strove for, and the two abodes — Hell for the one who transgressed and preferred this world, Paradise for the one who feared standing before his Lord and restrained himself from desire. Now a question is put to the Prophet ﷺ: *when* will that Hour arrive? The passage answers by taking the question apart. The timing is Allah's alone (42–44); the Prophet ﷺ was sent not to announce dates but to warn those who will fear it (45); and when the Day does come, the whole of worldly life will feel no longer than a single afternoon or morning (46). The demand for a date and the shrinking of a lifetime belong together: the passage opens with people treating the Hour as a distant curiosity and closes by showing how brief the distance will turn out to have been.

## A futile demand, and where knowledge of the Hour ends (ayat 42–44)

"They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ regarding the Hour, 'When will it be?'" Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes this as "the mala fide demand of the infidels" — a demand made in bad faith — that the Prophet ﷺ should tell them the exact date and time of the Day of Judgment. Its verdict on that demand is one word: futile. And the reply of the next two ayat shows why, because they were asking for something no created being has ever been given.

The reply comes in two steps, and together they close every door. First, addressed to the Prophet ﷺ himself: "But it is not for you to tell its time" — literally, "What do you have to mention of it?" Then the principle itself: *ilā rabbika muntahāhā*, "That knowledge rests with your Lord ˹alone˺" — its end-point, its final limit, is with Allah and no one else.

Ibn Kathir spells out how absolute this is: "its knowledge is not with you, nor with any creature. Rather the knowledge of it is with Allah. He is the One Who knows the exact time of its occurrence." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same in its own words: knowledge of the time and date is within Allah's own special prerogative, and His consummate wisdom "did not pass the information to any angel or Prophet ﷺ." Not the Prophet ﷺ, not any angel, not any creature at all.

Ibn Kathir connects this to the fuller statement in Sūrah al-Aʿrāf: "Heavy is its burden through the heavens and the earth. It shall not come upon you except all of a sudden. They ask you as if you have a good knowledge of it. Say: 'The knowledge thereof is with Allah'" (7:187). The Hour will not send advance notice; it comes all of a sudden.

Ibn Kathir also relates that when Jibril asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about the time of the last Hour, he replied: "The one questioned about it knows no more than the questioner." Even in that exchange — the angel of revelation asking, the recipient of revelation answering — the answer is the same: the knowledge is Allah's alone.

## Sent to warn, and a lifetime shrunk to half a day (ayat 45–46)

If the Prophet ﷺ was not given the date, what *was* he given? "Your duty is only to warn whoever is in awe of it." The Arabic opens with *innamā* — "only," a word of restriction: you are *only* a warner (*mundhir*), not a keeper of the calendar of the unseen.

Ibn Kathir unfolds the meaning as if Allah were saying to His Messenger: "I sent you to warn mankind and caution them to beware of the torment and punishment of Allah. So whoever fears Allah, fears standing before Him, and His threat, then he will follow you, and thus be successful and victorious. However, whoever denies you and opposes you, then he will only suffer loss and failure."

Notice who the warning is *for*: "whoever is in awe of it" — *man yakhshāhā*, from *khashyah*, reverent fear. The warning is sounded to everyone, but it lands in the heart that carries that fear. This ties the passage back to the sūrah's verdict a few ayat earlier: it was "him who feared standing before his Lord, and forbade himself from desire" (ayah 40) for whom Paradise was promised. The same fear that saves a person on that Day is the fear that lets the warning benefit him today. The scoffing questioner and the fearing believer hear identical words; only one of them is changed by them.

Then the passage — and the sūrah — ends with a stunning image, and it is the real answer to the question that opened it: "On the Day they see it, it will be as if they had stayed ˹in this world˺ no more than an afternoon or a morning."

Ibn Kathir explains: when people stand up from their graves and set out for the place of Gathering, the entire worldly life will feel short — "it will seem to them that it was only the afternoon of one day." He then relates the report of Ibn ʿAbbas (transmitted through Juwaybir from al-Dahhak) defining the two Arabic terms precisely: *ʿashiyyah* is the stretch from noon until sunset, and *duḥā* is the stretch from sunrise until noon. Qatadah adds that this is how the time period of the worldly life will look "in the eyes of the people when they see the Hereafter."

So the ayah is not saying time will literally have been short; it is describing how it will be *felt*. Decades of striving, accumulating, and delaying — and standing before the reality of the Hour, it will all compress into the length of a single morning or a single afternoon. Set that against the demand of ayah 42. They asked *when* the Hour would come, as though it were comfortably far away. The answer: however far it seems now, when you see it, your whole life will feel like it lasted from sunrise to noon.

## Living this passage

Two things follow directly from these ayat as the commentators present them.

First, certainty about the limits of knowledge. Allah did not pass the time of the Hour "to any angel or Prophet ﷺ," as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it — so any claim, in any age, to have calculated its date is a claim to what Allah withheld from every angel and Prophet. The believer simply repeats what the Prophet ﷺ said when Jibril asked him: the one questioned knows no more than the questioner.

Second, the right concern. The passage does not give the questioners a date; it tells them what the Prophet ﷺ was actually sent to do — to warn — and who the warning benefits: *whoever is in awe of it*. The real task, then, is to be among those people: to fear standing before one's Lord, to hold the self back from its desires, and to live this brief morning-and-afternoon of a life in a way that will bear the weight of the Day when it ends.

With this, Ibn Kathir closes: "This is the end of the Tafsir of Surat An-Nazi'at. And to Allah belongs all praise and thanks."
